subChunks.title: Modifying Rows — UPDATE SET WHERE
subChunks.hookHtml: The most dangerous four-word sequence in SQL is UPDATE table SET col without a WHERE clause — it silently changes every row in the table.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Syntax

UPDATE apprentices
SET    rank = 'Adept',
       xp   = xp + 500
WHERE  id = 1;

The cardinal rule: always include WHERE

An UPDATE without WHERE modifies every row. In production this is almost always wrong and often catastrophic. Always write the WHERE clause before writing the SET clause — make the filter the first thing you establish.

Updating multiple columns

UPDATE apprentices
SET rank = 'Mage', xp = 4800
WHERE name = 'Alice';

Computed updates

-- Add 100 XP to everyone in Apprentice rank:
UPDATE apprentices
SET    xp = xp + 100
WHERE  rank = 'Apprentice';

Verify before you run

-- Step 1: run as SELECT to check which rows match:
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Apprentice';

-- Step 2: satisfied? Run the UPDATE:
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE rank = 'Apprentice';

This select-before-update pattern is one of the most important production habits you can develop.

storyBeats.text: Alice passes her advancement exam. Her rank needs updating. Cipher writes nothing yet — first, he checks which rows will change.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Before every UPDATE, run the WHERE clause as a SELECT. See which rows you are about to change. Only then run the UPDATE. I have seen whole tables emptied with a well-intentioned UPDATE that forgot its WHERE clause. Do not be that archivist.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 XP bonus

All apprentices of rank 'Apprentice' have earned a 100 XP bonus. Write the UPDATE. Then SELECT their updated rows to verify.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Apprentice xp increased by 100
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (1,'Alice','Apprentice',1200),(2,'Bjorn','Adept',2400),(3,'Cassia','Mage',4800),(4,'Dorian','Novice',80),(5,'Elara','Archmage',7500),(6,'Fenrir','Apprentice',950);
guidedPracticeTests.overrideQuery: UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE rank = 'Apprentice'; SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Apprentice' ORDER BY name;
guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT name, xp FROM (SELECT 'Alice' AS name, 1300 AS xp UNION SELECT 'Fenrir', 1050) t ORDER BY name

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Update Alice (id=1) to rank 'Adept'. Then update ALL apprentices with xp >= 4000 to have their xp multiplied by 1.1 (rounded to integer). Write both UPDATE statements.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why always including a WHERE clause in UPDATE is critical, and describe the select-before-update pattern.

questions.prompt: What does `UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100` (no WHERE clause) do?
options: Adds 100 XP to every row in the apprentices table
Adds 100 XP to the first row only
Throws an error — WHERE is required for UPDATE
Adds 100 to the column definition's default
questions.answer: Adds 100 XP to every row in the apprentices table
questions.explanation: UPDATE without WHERE modifies every row. This is syntactically valid but almost always unintended in production.

questions.prompt: Which query correctly promotes Alice (id=1) to rank 'Adept' and sets her xp to 2500?
options: UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Adept', xp = 2500 WHERE id = 1
UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Adept' AND xp = 2500 WHERE id = 1
SET rank = 'Adept', xp = 2500 IN apprentices WHERE id = 1
questions.answer: UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Adept', xp = 2500 WHERE id = 1
questions.explanation: Multiple column updates are comma-separated in the SET clause. AND is not used inside SET — it is a logical operator for WHERE conditions.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of running `SELECT * FROM t WHERE condition` before `UPDATE t SET ... WHERE condition`?
options: To preview exactly which rows will be modified before committing the change
To lock the rows so other sessions cannot change them simultaneously
To check syntax of the WHERE clause
SELECT is required before every UPDATE by the SQL standard
questions.answer: To preview exactly which rows will be modified before committing the change
questions.explanation: The select-before-update pattern lets you visually confirm the row set before modifying it. It is a safety habit, not a technical requirement — but it prevents many production accidents.

questions.prompt: A developer updates a status column to 'archived' but accidentally omits the WHERE clause. What is the quickest recovery if the database has no recent backup?
options: Rollback — if the UPDATE was inside an open transaction that has not yet been committed
Run a reverse UPDATE setting all rows back
Use UNDO if the engine supports it
No recovery is possible without a backup
questions.answer: Rollback — if the UPDATE was inside an open transaction that has not yet been committed
questions.explanation: If the UPDATE ran inside an uncommitted transaction (BEGIN / START TRANSACTION), ROLLBACK reverses it entirely. If already committed without a transaction, recovery requires a backup or point-in-time restore. This is why wrapping destructive statements in transactions is a professional habit.
